title: "Getting started"

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

This page runs the complete SIGNAL workflow on the simulated example data that
ships with the package. It takes about a minute.

```{r}
library(SIGNAL)
data(SIGNAL_example)
str(SIGNAL_example, max.level = 1)
table(SIGNAL_example$gene_type)
```

The example has 70 genes on 400 cells of four cell types (`CT1`–`CT4`):
40 null genes, 10 cell-type genes, 10 spatial genes (high in a hotspot for all
cell types) and 10 ctSVGs (high in the hotspot for `CT1` only).

## Step 1: create a SIGNAL object

SIGNAL needs three inputs:

* `counts`: a genes $\times$ cells matrix of raw counts (base or sparse matrix);
* `location`: a cells $\times$ 2 matrix of spatial coordinates;
* `celltype`: one cell-type label per cell, or a cells $\times$ cell types
  matrix of cell-type proportions (for spot-level data).

```{r}
obj <- createSIGNALobject(counts = SIGNAL_example$counts,
                          location = SIGNAL_example$location,
                          celltype = SIGNAL_example$celltype)
obj
```

## Step 2: filter and transform expression

Genes expressed in fewer than `min_cells` cells are removed. Each gene is then
converted to normal scores, `qnorm((rank(y) - 0.5) / n)`; tied counts share
their average rank.

**Sparse data with many zeros:** all zeros of a gene then share one score,
which can make the spatial test anti-conservative. For such data use
`transform = "impute"`, which breaks tied zeros at random and averages the
scores over `n_imp` draws (`seed` makes it reproducible).

```{r}
obj <- SIGNAL_preprocess(obj, min_cells = 10, seed = 1)
```

## Step 3: build the kernels

The **cell-type kernel** is a Hamming kernel for cell-type labels and a
Gaussian kernel for cell-type proportions (`celltype_distance = "auto"`). The
**spatial kernels** are 11 kernels at different scales: 5 Gaussian, 5 Matérn
and a thin-plate spline. With more than 6,000 cells, SIGNAL uses a single
Gaussian kernel instead (see [Large data](Parallel.html)).

```{r}
obj <- SIGNAL_kernel(obj)
names(obj@spatial_kernels)
```

## Step 4: test the genes

`SIGNAL_test()` runs the overall test and the three component tests for every
gene and kernel, and combines the p-values over the 11 kernels with the Cauchy
combination test.

```{r}
obj <- SIGNAL_test(obj, ncores = 2, verbose = FALSE)
head(obj@result)
```

The result is a table with one row per gene and the four p-values, not
adjusted for multiple testing. Save it with `write.csv(obj@result, "signal.csv")`.

The share of genes of each true type with p < 0.05:

```{r}
type <- SIGNAL_example$gene_type[rownames(obj@result)]
round(apply(obj@result < 0.05, 2, function(x) tapply(x, type, mean)), 2)
```

Null genes are rarely detected. The cell-type genes are found by the cell-type
test, the spatial genes by the spatial test and the ctSVGs by the ctSVG test.
Most ctSVGs are also found by the cell-type test: higher expression in the
hotspot for `CT1` only also raises `CT1`'s average expression.

### Classifying genes

A common rule is to call a gene spatially variable when its BH-adjusted
overall p-value is below 0.05, and then label it with every effect whose
component p-value is below 0.05:

```{r}
res <- obj@result
res$padj_overall <- p.adjust(res$p_overall, "BH")
sig <- res$padj_overall < 0.05
category <- ifelse(!sig, "Not significant",
  apply(res[, c("p_celltype", "p_spatial", "p_ctSVG")] < 0.05, 1, function(f)
    paste(c("CellType", "Spatial", "ctSVG")[f], collapse = "+")))
table(truth = type, SIGNAL = category)
```

## Step 5: visualise genes

```{r, fig.height = 3}
SIGNAL_plotGene(obj, "gene51")
```

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
SIGNAL_plotGene(obj, "gene61", by_celltype = TRUE)
```

`gene51` (a spatial gene) is high in the hotspot for every cell type;
`gene61` (a ctSVG) only for `CT1`.

## Step 6: find the cell types behind each ctSVG

`SIGNAL_celltype()` tests each gene once per cell type, using an interaction
kernel built from that cell type alone.

```{r}
ctsvg <- rownames(obj@result)[obj@result$p_ctSVG < 0.05]
obj <- SIGNAL_celltype(obj, genes = ctsvg, ncores = 2, verbose = FALSE)
signif(head(obj@celltype_result), 2)
```

The small p-values are in the `CT1` column, the cell type that carries the
simulated pattern.

## One-step analysis

`SIGNAL()` runs steps 1–4 in one call:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
obj <- SIGNAL(counts, location, celltype, seed = 1)
```

## Options

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `transform` | `"rank"` | `"impute"` breaks tied zeros at random; recommended for sparse data with many zeros |
| `method` | `"davies"` | tail probabilities: `"davies"`, `"saddlepoint"` (accurate below 1e-6), `"liu"` (fast approximation), `"davies_liu"` |
| `ncores` | all available cores | number of parallel workers (Linux and macOS) |
| `parallel` | `"auto"` | split the work over genes (`"genes"`) or kernels (`"kernels"`) |
| `approximation` | `"auto"` | one Gaussian spatial kernel above `max_cells = 6000` cells |
| `celltype_distance` | `"auto"` | Hamming for labels, Euclidean (Gaussian kernel) for proportions |
